Using valence bond theory, compare [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and [FeF₆]³⁻ with respect to (a) the type of hybridisation, (b) the magnetic behaviour and (c) whether each is an inner or outer orbital complex. (Atomic number of Fe = 26)

Differentiate between SN1 and SN2 reactions on the basis of (a) the number of steps in the mechanism, (b) the order of the reaction and (c) the stereochemistry of the product. Give one example of an alkyl halide that reacts mainly by each mechanism.

Carbohydrates are the main source of energy in our food. Glucose, a monosaccharide, exists mostly in a cyclic form. Two monosaccharide units join through an oxygen atom to form a disaccharide such as sucrose, maltose or lactose. Sugars that reduce Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution are called reducing sugars. Starch, the storage polysaccharide of plants, is a mixture of two components, amylose and amylopectin, while cellulose forms the cell walls of plants.
(a) What name is given to the linkage that joins two monosaccharide units?
(b) Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar while maltose is a reducing sugar?
(c) Write two structural differences between amylose and amylopectin.
OR
(c) Name the products obtained on the hydrolysis of (i) sucrose and (ii) lactose. Why is sucrose called invert sugar?

A fuel cell is a galvanic cell that converts the energy of combustion of a fuel directly into electrical energy. In the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen gases are bubbled through porous carbon electrodes into a concentrated aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide. The cell runs as long as the gases are supplied, and the only product is water. Such cells were used to provide electrical power in the Apollo space programme, and the water produced was used by the astronauts for drinking.
(a) Write the reactions taking place at the anode and at the cathode of this cell.
(b) Write the overall cell reaction.
(c) State two advantages of a fuel cell over a thermal power plant.
OR
(c) How is a fuel cell different from a primary cell such as a dry cell? Give two points.

(a) An organic compound A (C₃H₆O) does not reduce Tollens' reagent but gives a yellow precipitate with iodine and sodium hydroxide. On reduction, A gives compound B (C₃H₈O), which on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid gives compound C (C₃H₆). Identify A, B and C and write the equations for the reactions involved.
(b) Give one chemical test each to distinguish between (i) benzaldehyde and acetophenone and (ii) ethanal and propanal.
OR
(a) Arrange the following in increasing order of acid strength and give a reason: CH₃COOH, ClCH₂COOH, FCH₂COOH, Cl₂CHCOOH.
(b) Why are carboxylic acids higher boiling than alcohols of comparable molecular mass?
(c) Write the equations for (i) the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction and (ii) the decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate.

(a) Write the IUPAC names of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] and K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃].
(b) Draw the crystal field splitting diagram for an octahedral complex. Write the electronic configuration of a d⁴ ion when (i) Δ₀ > P and (ii) Δ₀ < P.
(c) What type of isomerism is shown by [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ and [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br? Give a chemical test to distinguish between them.
OR
(a) What is meant by the chelate effect? Give one example of a chelating ligand.
(b) Draw the geometrical isomers of [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺. Which of them is optically active?
(c) Explain why [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is coloured while [Sc(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is colourless.

Assertion (A): The rate of a reaction generally increases when the temperature is raised.
Reason (R): At a higher temperature, a larger fraction of the molecules has energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

Assertion (A): Tertiary alkyl halides react fastest by the SN2 mechanism.
Reason (R): The rate of an SN2 reaction decreases as the crowding around the carbon bearing the halogen increases.
What is an ideal solution? State two of its characteristics and give one example.
Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease on dilution, whereas its molar conductivity increases?

(a) [Cr(NH₃)₃Cl₃]

(a) The boiling point of ethanol is higher than that of methoxymethane.

Identify the compounds A, B and C in the following sequence of reactions and write the equations:

(a) Write two structural differences between DNA and RNA.
(b) What type of bonding stabilises the α-helix structure of a protein?
(c) What happens when a protein is denatured? Give one example.

Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes very slowly at room temperature. When a small amount of potassium iodide solution is added, the decomposition becomes rapid and bubbles of oxygen are seen at once. If the mixture is warmed, the reaction becomes faster still. Chemists explain these observations by saying that molecules must collide with a certain minimum energy before they can react, and that only a fraction of the collisions are effective.
(a) Define the activation energy of a reaction.
(b) How does potassium iodide increase the rate of this reaction? Does it change the enthalpy change of the reaction?
(c) Write the Arrhenius equation and state what each term in it represents.
OR
(c) The decomposition follows first order kinetics with a half-life of 20 minutes under certain conditions. How long will it take for the concentration of hydrogen peroxide to fall to one-eighth of its initial value?

Ethanol is produced on a large scale by the fermentation of the sugar present in molasses, sugarcane or fruits. The process is carried out by yeast in the absence of air. The ethanol sold for industrial use is made unfit for drinking by adding substances such as copper sulphate and pyridine. Methanol, which is sometimes present in illicit liquor, is highly poisonous and can cause blindness and death even in small amounts.
(a) Name the two enzymes, present in yeast, that take part in the conversion of sugar into ethanol.
(b) What is ethanol called after copper sulphate and pyridine have been added to it? Why are they added?
(c) What product is obtained when ethanol is oxidised with (i) pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) and (ii) acidified potassium dichromate in excess?
OR
(c) Describe a chemical test to distinguish between methanol and ethanol and write the equation involved.

(a) State Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
(b) A current of 2 A is passed through a solution of silver nitrate for 30 minutes. Calculate the mass of silver deposited at the cathode. (Atomic mass of Ag = 108 u, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
(c) Name the products formed at the cathode and at the anode when (i) an aqueous solution of sodium chloride and (ii) dilute sulphuric acid are electrolysed using platinum electrodes.
OR
(a) Write the reactions taking place at the anode and at the cathode of a lead storage battery when it is in use.
(b) What happens when the battery is recharged?
(c) The resistance of a conductivity cell filled with a KCl solution of conductivity 1.29 × 10⁻² S cm⁻¹ is 100 Ω. Calculate the cell constant.

(a) Write the mechanism of the acid-catalysed hydration of ethene to ethanol.
(b) Explain Williamson's synthesis of ethers with one example. Why can tert-butyl ethyl ether not be prepared from tert-butyl bromide and sodium ethoxide?
(c) Write the equation for Kolbe's reaction.
OR
(a) How will you convert (i) phenol to benzene, (ii) ethanol to ethanal and (iii) anisole to phenol?
(b) Arrange the following in increasing order of acid strength and give a reason: phenol, p-nitrophenol, p-cresol.
(c) Give one chemical test to distinguish between phenol and ethanol.

(a) State Raoult's law for a solution of two volatile liquids. What is meant by positive deviation from Raoult's law? Give one example and explain the cause of the deviation.
(b) The vapour pressures of pure liquids A and B at a certain temperature are 400 mm Hg and 600 mm Hg respectively. If the total vapour pressure of their solution is 520 mm Hg, find the mole fraction of each liquid in the solution and the mole fraction of A in the vapour phase.
OR
(a) What is the van't Hoff factor? What is its value for a solute that associates in solution?

(c) Why is a 1 M solution of NaCl expected to show a greater depression in freezing point than a 1 M solution of glucose?
